title: Customer Churn Analysis — Verified Findings Report
executive_summary: Across 749 customers, 37.65% churned, paying an average monthly fee of $42.11. Churn is strikingly insensitive to plan tier (36.60%–38.87%) but highly sensitive to contract type: Monthly customers churn at 48.32% versus 21.85% for Annual, a 121.11% relative increase. The newest signup cohort (2024) churns most at 39.83%. A high-risk segment of 100 customers with 5+ support tickets and satisfaction ≤ 2 churns at 71%. Lifetime value, unlike churn, scales sharply with plan: Premium customers are worth 292.01% more than Basic.

key_findings.statement: The cleaned dataset contains 749 customers, of whom 37.65% churned; the average monthly fee is $42.11.
Churn varies little across plans — Basic 38.87%, Standard 36.68%, Premium 36.60% — only a 2.27 percentage-point spread between the highest (Basic) and lowest (Premium) tier.
Cohort churn is broadly stable with an uptick among the newest signups: 2021 38.02%, 2022 36.74%, 2023 37.05%, 2024 39.83%; 2024 sits 3.09 percentage points above the lowest cohort (2022).
Contract type is the dominant churn factor: Monthly 48.32% versus Annual 21.85%, a 26.47 percentage-point gap — Monthly churn is 121.11% higher, about 2.21x the Annual rate.
The at-risk segment — 100 customers (13.4% of the base) with support_tickets ≥ 5 and satisfaction ≤ 2 — churns at 71%, roughly 1.89x the overall rate and the clearest intervention target.
Mean tenure is 20.81 months (median 19, SD 13.25); mean satisfaction is 3.42, with 27 customers (3.6%) missing a satisfaction score.
Lifetime value rises steeply by tier: Basic $463.46, Standard $868.83 (1.87x Basic), Premium $1,816.78 (3.92x Basic, a 292.01% increase).

limitations: Churn is measured at a single snapshot; newer cohorts have had less time to churn, so cohort comparisons mix tenure effects with cohort effects.
Satisfaction scores are missing for 27 customers; satisfaction-based metrics and the at-risk filter exclude them.
Results are associational, not causal — annual contracts may attract inherently loyal customers rather than directly reduce churn.
Group churn differences (plan, cohort) were not tested for statistical significance, and the at-risk thresholds (5 tickets, satisfaction ≤ 2) are analyst-chosen cutoffs.
conclusion: Overall churn of 37.65% is high. The strongest levers are contract mix and the at-risk segment: shifting Monthly customers toward Annual contracts and proactively engaging the 100 high-ticket, low-satisfaction customers (71% churn) offer the largest retention gains. Plan tier barely moves churn but multiplies lifetime value, so upselling remains a revenue, not retention, strategy.
